Discrete distributions chapter

Discrete distributions: evaluated written-course pool

Search boundary and selection

Nine university candidates were compared using course inventories and accessible chapter text. Five courses were actually read. Oxford, Cambridge, Berkeley and MIT form the core; Stanford supplies an application extension. Selection follows chapter-level scientific coverage, derivation quality, support and parameter clarity, computational interpretation and accessible written evidence. An inventory, title or download is not counted as a lecture reading. This is a bounded documented search; it is not possible to certify that every course worldwide has been evaluated or that four courses are globally best.

Priority Course and attribution Actual reading Chapter role and limitations
Core, structural proof Oxford Prelims Probability, James Martin, Michaelmas 2019 Native PDF pages 18–26 and 39–44, read completely Parameter contracts, geometric first-step moments, PGF uniqueness, sums, random-sum composition and thinning. The geometric support starts at one. The random-urn example's final expectation line uses an inconsistent capital N; its model uses the stated lowercase n.
Core, waiting and rare-event derivations Berkeley CS 70, Rao and Walrand, Spring 2016, Note19 in Fall 2016 archive All eight pages read, including both halves of the Poisson-limit proof Tail-sum proof, geometric factorial moments, coupon stages, Poisson moments and limits. Its single-peak wording omits the tied modes at a positive integer parameter. Average arrival rate alone cannot identify a Poisson law.
Core, precise building blocks MIT 18.05 Spring 2022; course instructors Jeremy Orloff and Jennifer French Kamrin; written-note authors Jeremy Orloff and Jonathan Bloom Combined PDF pages34–51; the initially truncated pages42–43 were reread separately Independent sequence grouping, binomial moments, failure-based geometric convention and explicit convolution. The neutral stopping probability must be distinguished from the probability of an event colloquially called success. The binomial-table sentence has a parameter-letter typo; the formula uses n,p.
Additional, application and model criticism Stanford CS 109, Chris Piech, Winter 2022, Lecture 8 All 66 native textual slides read; progressive duplicated slides recognized Poisson limits, rate units, corruption counts, tail computation and model change. Although the lecture landing page advertises geometric/negative-binomial objectives, the acquired slide deck only summarizes them; it is not counted as a detailed derivation of those laws. Slide65's fixed-n Poisson description is corrected; finite fixed-n counts are bounded. Heuristic approximation thresholds and mild-dependence claims are not universal guarantees.
Core, complete model catalogue Cambridge Introduction to Probability, 2023–24 Lecture 4, Mateja Jamnik and Thomas Sauerwald All 23 native PDF pages read after a bounded retry succeeded Negative-binomial stopped counts and sums, hypergeometric samples and moments. The broad hypergeometric range is refined to its positive-mass support. Finite Poisson-process intervals are not literally Bernoulli trials; the small-interval approximation is stated correctly.
Screened extension CMU36-700 Fall 2016, Siva Balakrishnan Lecture 4 inventory and common-law section already evaluated in the preceding chapter; not counted as a new full reading here Useful MGF comparison, but does not replace this chapter's waiting/support derivations.
Screened extension ETH Zurich Probability Theory FS2020, Johanna F.Ziegel Previously verified written-course inventory; no additional discrete-distribution pages read here Not counted as a chapter reading.
Screened extension Harvard Stat110, Joe Blitzstein; book by Blitzstein and Hwang Official free-book inventory verified; no book chapters read in this delivery Course title or textbook availability alone is not a synthesis contribution.
Screened extension Cornell CS2800 Fall2017 Previously inspected expectation lecture establishes context Not a complete named-distribution catalogue; not counted here.

Synthesis decisions

Oxford supplies the algebraic framework; Berkeley derives infinite waiting laws; MIT reconciles fixed horizons and counting conventions; Cambridge fills the negative-binomial and hypergeometric catalogue; Stanford supplies engineering applications and examples of model assumptions failing. Full stopped-sequence, subset-count and finite-population waiting proofs develop the displayed formulas. These derivations are verified independently by exhaustive finite enumeration and symbolic identities.

The source discrepancy register is part of the lesson: positive and zero-based geometric conventions are both stated; two Poisson modes occur when the positive parameter is an integer; rate must be multiplied by exposure; finite binomial counts remain distinct from unbounded Poisson limits; a shared random probability changes the law and variance; and independence is never inferred merely from identical marginal probabilities.

Original Iranian examination bridges

The original rendered PhDCS1404 PDF page15 and MSCE1405 PDF page8 were visually reinspected in this chapter. The relevant binomial and posterior-geometric questions are explicitly reused for deeper distribution analysis; they are not newly discovered unique archive entries. Ordered printed alternatives, immutable repository commit, page numbers, PDF hashes and independently derived answers remain inspectable. No official answer key is claimed.
